findings.text: The first lines tell a newcomer what Athena is and what makes it different. Those two sentences are all the page says about Athena. Everything after them is about another project.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page explains why it exists: the study is a demonstration of Athena. A newcomer who came to the Athena site can see why they are reading about firstmate.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: What to do next is linked from the top and easy to find. But the install step assumes the reader already has a checkout, gives no clone command, and lists no prerequisites such as a Rust toolchain or model API keys before `athena ask`.
findings.source: Header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself"; Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh"

findings.text: Firstmate gets a clear one-sentence definition, and the next section says why it matters: workers don't overwrite each other's files, and nobody has to start each agent by hand.
findings.source: Start here: "Firstmate is a tool that keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a separate AI coding tool, called a worker, so that several tasks can run side by side."

findings.text: Defining jargon (captain, yolo, green, red) before it is used helps a newcomer. The cost is that the same definitions appear twice, which makes a long page longer.
findings.source: Words used first: "These words appear in the sentences that follow. Each is defined here, and again in the Glossary at the end of the page."

findings.text: The two definitions of captain don't match. The glossary version is narrower and leaves out that the captain directs firstmate.
findings.source: Glossary, captain: "The person who approves every PR merge and every local-only landing when yolo is off." vs Words used first: "The person who directs firstmate and decides whether finished work is merged."

findings.text: Saying openly that the source has a gap is honest. Still, a newcomer is left unsure when firstmate merges work on its own, which is one of the main behaviours the page describes.
findings.source: in scope: "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: Almost every sentence carries several claim links. They back up the traceability promise, but they make the text harder to read for someone who just wants to understand it.
findings.source: Most bullets end in several links, e.g. "[c2] [c10] [c12] [c17] [c21]"

findings.text: The States, Counters and Transitions sections read like a state-machine spec, with ids such as t9 and exit codes 75 and 1. A technical reader can follow them, but they are heavy for a first visit and go well past what a newcomer needs.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: This describes how the study was produced, not what firstmate does. A newcomer can't tell why it matters to them, although it does make clear that nothing was run.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths: ..."

findings.text: This section doesn't say which repository holds the `studies/` folder, so a newcomer can't find the source data from it without guessing.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
